session.title: Cornucopianism vs. Simonism: Does Wikipedia misrepresent Julian Simon?
session.question: Does cornucopianism as described on Wikipedia conflict with a closer reading of Julian Simon, whose actual position may be that the category of 'natural resource' is incoherent (they're just resources), not simply that we will not run out?

sources.title: The Ultimate Resource 2
sources.found_via: anna-mcp book search for 'Julian Simon The Ultimate Resource'
sources.status_detail: Deep-read via sub-agent. Key findings: Simon explicitly rejects cornucopian label; argues resources are services not substances; finiteness is a category error; resources are human-created not nature-given
sources.relevance: Primary source for Simon's actual position on resources, human ingenuity, and what constitutes a 'resource'

sources.title: Cornucopianism (Wikipedia)
sources.found_via: Direct fetch — the Wikipedia page the research question references
sources.status_detail: Defines cornucopianism as belief that technology ensures unlimited supply; calls Simon 'one of the best-known cornucopian thinkers'; doesn't distinguish Simon's nuanced position from broader label
sources.relevance: The target of the research question — does this page accurately represent Simon?

sources.title: There Are No Natural Resources (Boudreaux on Simon's 'ultimate resource')
sources.found_via: Web search for Simon's views on natural resources as a category
sources.status_detail: Boudreaux argues Simon's position is that materials only become 'resources' through human creativity — nature creates materials, not resources
sources.relevance: Directly articulates the 'Simonist' view that the category of natural resource is incoherent — closest to the research question's thesis

sources.title: There Are No Natural Resources
sources.found_via: Web search for Simon's argument that natural resources are not natural
sources.status_detail: Same Boudreaux argument, possibly republished — human mind as 'ultimate resource', materials ≠ resources without human innovation
sources.relevance: Reinforces the Simonist interpretation that resources are human-created, not nature-given

sources.title: A Reply to My Critics
sources.found_via: Web search results for Simon's own writings
sources.status_detail: Simon argues: resource stock must be measured by price not quantity; finiteness is not testable; substitutability is increasing, not infinite at any moment; critics distort his positions
sources.relevance: Simon's own words correcting mischaracterizations — key for understanding his actual position vs popular labels

sources.title: Julian Simon, 'Natural Resources are Infinite'
sources.found_via: Web search — appears to be an extract from Simon used in an environmental ethics course
sources.status_detail: Simon argues people create resources; market pricing signals substitution; historical trend of declining real costs
sources.relevance: Simon's own argument in accessible form — relevant to whether he merely claims abundance or redefines what a resource is
